translations.text: We begin to tell the history of the kings of the Georgians, and of their first fathers and kindred. Chapter One: The story of the eight brothers. First let us record this:
The Armenians and the Georgians, the Ranians and the Movakanians, the Heretians and the Lekians, the Mingrelians and the Caucasians: all of these had one father, named Targamos.
This Targamos was the son of Tarshi, the grandson of Japheth, the son of Noah. This Targamos was a mighty man, a hero.
After the division of languages, when they built the tower at Babylon, the languages were divided there, and from there people were scattered over all the earth.
This Targamos came with his kindred and settled between two mountains that no one could climb, Ararat and Masis. His kindred was great and
beyond counting, for he had many wives, and sons and daughters, and children and grandchildren from his sons and daughters, because he lived six hundred years.
The land of Ararat and Masis could no longer hold them. The land that had fallen to him as his lot had these borders:
on the east the Sea of Gurgan, on the west the Pontic Sea, on the south the Sea of Oreti, and on the north the Caucasus mountain.
Among his children eight men stood out, mighty and famous heroes, whose names are these:
The first was called Haos, the second Kartlos, the third Bardos, the fourth Movakan, the fifth Lek, the sixth Heros, the seventh Kavkas, and the eighth Egros. These eight were heroes.
But Haos was the greatest hero of them all, for no one like him had ever existed, either before the Flood or after it, in stature, strength and courage.
Since the land of Ararat and Masis could no longer hold them, Targamos divided his land and his kindred among these eight heroes.
He gave half of his kindred, and half of his land, the better half, to Haos. To the other seven he gave their portions according to their [?]:
He led those seven toward the north and divided the lands among them according to their worth. He gave land to Kartlos and set its borders: on the east Hereti and the Berduji river;
on the west the Pontic Sea; on the south the mountain that runs along the head of the Berduji river, and the mountain that runs toward the west,
whose waters flow down northward and join the Mtkvari (Kura), the mountain that runs between Klarjeti and Tao as far as the sea; and on the north
the border is Ghado, a small mountain that comes out from the Caucasus as a spur, whose tip touches the end of Ghado, which is now called Likhi.
He gave Kartlos everything within these borders. To Bardos he gave the land south of the Mtkvari, from the Berduji river to where the Mtkvari and the Rakhsi (Araxes) meet.
This Bardos built the city of Bardavi and settled there. To Movakan he gave the land north of the Mtkvari, from the mouth of the Little Alazani to the sea.
He built the city of Movakaneti and settled there.
To Heros he gave the land north of the Mtkvari, from the mouth of the Little Alazani to Tqetba, which is now called Gulgula.
This Heros was the first to build a city, at the confluence of the two Alazani rivers.
He gave it his own name, Hereti, and that is why Hereti is called Hereti. That place is now called Khoranta.
To Egros he gave the land along the bay of the sea, and set its borders: on the east the small mountain that is now called Likhi;
on the west the sea; on the north the river of Little Khazaria, where the tip of the Caucasus comes to an end.
And Egros built a city and called it by his own name, Egrisi. That place is now called Bedia.
North of the Caucasus was not Targamos's portion; in fact, there was no one at all living north of the Caucasus.
That land was uninhabited from the Caucasus as far as the great river that flows into the Sea of Darubandi (Derbent).
So he brought out two of the many giants, Lekan and Kavkas.
He gave Lekan the land from the Sea of Darubandi to the river Lomeki, and north as far as the great river
of Khazaria. And he gave Kavkas the land from the river Lomeki to the end of the Caucasus, in the west.
Haos settled in the dwellings of his father Targamos and held the land to the north, as I have written:
on the south from Mount Oreti, on the east as far as the Sea of Gurgan, and on the west as far as the Pontic Sea.
Haos was governor and lord over these seven giants, and all of them were subject to Haos.
And all eight of them together served the giant Nimrod, who was the first king of the whole earth.
A few years after this, Haos summoned the seven giants, gathered them, and said to them: "God Most High has given us strength and has made our people numerous.
Now, with the help of the Creator, let us be no one's slaves, and let us serve no one but God the Creator."
The seven giants agreed and confirmed that plan. They rebelled against Nimrod and paid him no more tribute.
They spoke with certain other peoples, and those other peoples also became disloyal.
Then Nimrod grew angry. He gathered his giants and all the troops who obeyed him,
and marched against the Targamosians. Haos summoned all seven giants and the whole people of Targamos.
Certain other western peoples also came to help them. Haos gathered all of these and took up position at the foot of Masis.
When Nimrod reached the land of Adarbadagan, he halted there and sent sixty giants, and strong troops with them, to fight the Targamosians.
When Nimrod's troops arrived, the seven giants, the brothers of Haos, went out to meet them with a strong army.
Haos, with an even stronger army, stood behind them at their rear. A fierce battle broke out between them, like the fury of a storm in the sky.
The dust from their feet was like a thick cloud; the flashing of their weapons
was like lightning in the sky; the noise of their voices was like the sound of thunder;
their arrows and slung stones were as many as dense hail, and their blood poured out like the torrents after hailstorms.
The battle between them grew fiercer, and countless men fell on both sides.
Haos stood behind his giants, giving them strength and encouraging them with a terrifying voice that was like the crash of a thunderbolt.
Then the Targamosians won, and they destroyed those sixty giants of Nimrod and their armies.
But these seven Targamosian giants, Kartlos, Bardos, Movakan, Heros, Lekan, Kavkasos and Egros, survived without wounds, and, crowned with victory, they gave thanks to God.
When Nimrod heard of this, he grew angry and marched against them with all his might.
Haos did not have as many troops as Nimrod's troops, so he fortified himself in the ravines of Masis.
Nimrod came up against him from below. He was armored in iron and bronze from his feet to the crown of his head.
He climbed up on a hill to parley with Haos, and he spoke to him again about submitting to him, hoping that Haos would be willing to come back over to him.
But Haos said to his giants: "Guard my flank from behind, and I will go up close to Nimrod."
He went out and came face to face with Nimrod, close to him, and shot an arrow. It struck Nimrod in the chest, on his bronze breastplate, and passed out through his back.
Then Nimrod fell, and his camp fled. And the kindred of Targamos were set free.
Then Haos made himself king over his brothers, and also over the other peoples near his borders.
These seven brothers each went to his own land, and they were subject to Haos. Up to this point we have written the story of all eight brothers.
Chapter Two. The Story of Kartli. From here on let us begin and tell the story of Kartli and of its people, and their history up to our own days,
and how Targamos divided the land among his kindred and all eight of his sons. He gave Kartlos the land that we described above.
This Kartlos first came to the place where the Aragvi joins the Mtkvari, and he went up onto the mountain that is called Armazi.
He first built fortifications on it, built himself a house up there, and called that mountain Kartli, after his own name.
Until the idol Armazi was set up there, the mountain was called Kartli, and because of it all of Kartli, from Khunani to the Sea of Sper, was called Kartli.
After this, the same Kartlos built the fortress of Orbi, which is now called Samshvilde.
He also built the Mtveri fortress, which is now called Khunani. He lived for many years, and his descendants multiplied.
Among his sons five giants stood out, whose names are these: the first Mtskhetos, the second Gardabos, the third Kakhos, the fourth Kukhos, the fifth Gachios.
All five of them were giants, but Mtskhetos was the mightiest of them.
Kartlos died, and they buried him on the summit of Kartli, which is now called Armazi. After this his wife built Dedatsikhe.
She also built Bostan-kalaki, which is now called Rustavi. And the wife of Kartlos divided the land among all five of those giants, her sons.
To Gardabos she gave Khunani, and she set its boundaries: on the east the Berduji River, on the west the city of Gachiani, on the south the mountain mentioned earlier, and on the north the Mtkvari.
To Gachios she gave the fortress of Orbi and the land from the Skvireti River up to the head of the Abotsi.
This Gachios built the city of Gachiani, which was then called the Hunting City.

And to Kukhos she gave Bostan-kalaki, which is now called Rustavi. She gave him the land from the Aragvi as far as Hereti, ... as far as the confluence [?], between the mountain of Kakheti and the Mtkvari.
And to Kakhos she gave the land between the Caucasus and the mountain of Kakheti, from the Aragvi as far as Tketbadi, which is the border of Hereti.
And this Kakhos built Cheleti, and Kukhos helped in the building of Cheleti, for the chief fortress was the portion of Kakhos.
And [?] was given to Kakhos for the help, and he helped in the building of Cheleti, which was called Ber [?], the first built in Kakheti.
And Mtskhetos, who was the mightiest hero among his brothers, remained in the dwellings of their father Kartlos, the place that is now called Armazi.
And he also built a city at the confluence of the Mtkvari and the Aragvi, and called it by his own name, Mtskheta.
And he held the land from Tbilisi and the Aragvi westward as far as the Sea of Speri.
And he was ruler and lord over all four brothers, and all four were subject to him.
These are the portions of the sons of Kartlos, which their mother divided among them after the death of Kartlos.
And the son of Kartlos lived for many years and many ages, and his kindred multiplied, and the kindred of all of them multiplied.
And among the children of Mtskhetos there appeared three famous heroes, whose names are these:
the first Uplos, the next Odzrkhos, and the third Javakhos. He divided the land and all the ten [?] kindreds among them.
To Odzrkhos he gave the land from Tasiskari as far as the Sea of Speri, a rocky land. This Odzrkhos built two fortified cities: Odzrkhe and Tukharisi.
And to Javakhos he gave the land from Panavari as far as the source of the Mtkvari.
And this Javakhos built two fortified cities: Tsunda and the city of Artaani, which was then called the City of the Kajis and is now called Huri.
And Uplos remained in the dwelling of their father Mtskhetos, in Mtskheta. And he held the land from the Aragvi and from Tbilisi as far as Tasiskari and Panavari.
And he built Uplistsikhe, Urbnisi and Kaspi. The land from the Aragvi and from Armazi as far as Tasiskari he called Zena-sopeli, which is now called Shida Kartli.
And until the death of Mtskhetos, all these descendants of Targamos lived in love with one another.
And they were afraid of the Nimrodites, for they expected the Nimrodites to seek vengeance for the blood of Nimrod.
And they hastened to strengthen their fortified cities out of fear of the Nimrodites.
But when Mtskhetos, son of Kartlos, died, envy arose among the descendants of Kartlos, and they began to fight and quarrel with one another.
For they would not obey Uplos, son of Mtskhetos, nor call him lord, though he had been left on the throne of Kartlos, since his father had given him lordship over the descendants of Kartlos.

They began to fight and quarrel with one another, and the fighting among them went on for a long time. At times two of these kindreds would rise up against one, and others would help one side or another.
And at other times others would rise up against one another, and still others would help them. At times there was peace among them, and then again they would fall out and fight.
And this state of affairs went on among them for a long time, and none among them was more eminent or more renowned than the rest; instead, local lords rose up in place after place.
And whoever was in Mtskheta was the chief over all the others.
They were called neither king nor duke (eristavi); instead they were called the head of the household (mamasakhlisi). He was the peacemaker and judge for the other descendants of Kartlos.
For the city of Mtskheta had grown greater than all the others, and they called it the mother-city.
At that time they forgot God, their Creator, and became worshippers of the sun, the moon and the five stars. Their firmest and greatest oath was by the tomb of Kartlos.
The Coming of the Khazars. At that time the Khazars grew strong and began to make war on the peoples of Lek and Kavkas. At that time all these descendants of Targamos lived in peace and mutual love.
Durdzuk, son of Tiret, was lord over the sons of Kavkas. They sent word to all six peoples descended from Targamos and asked for help against the Khazars.
All the peoples descended from Targamos gathered and crossed the Caucasus mountains.
They plundered all the borderlands of Khazaria, built cities on the frontier of Khazaria, and came back.
After this the Khazars appointed a king, and all the Khazars submitted to the king they had appointed.
They followed his lead and came out through the Sea Gate, which is now called Darubandi (Derbent).
The descendants of Targamos could not resist them, for the Khazars were countless in number. They plundered the land of the descendants of Targamos and destroyed all

the cities of Ararat, of Masis and of the north. The fortified cities that remained to them were Tukharisi, Samshvilde, and Mtveris-tsikhe, which is Khunani, as well as Inner Kartli (Shida Kartli) and Egrisi.
The Khazars learned both of these routes: the Sea Gate, which is Darubandi, and the Aragvi Gate, which is Dariala (Daryal).
The Khazars came out and raided more and more often, and they could no longer resist them. From then on all these descendants of Targamos became tributaries of the Khazars.
Now when the king of the Khazars first came out, plundered the lands I have written about above, and crossed back over the Caucasus mountains,
he had a son named Uobos, and he gave his son captives from Armenia (Somkhiti) and Kartli.
He also gave him land, part of the territory of Kavkas, west of the Lomeki river (the Terek) as far as the western end of the mountains.
Uobos (here spelled Utbos) settled there. His descendants are the Ossetians, and that is Ossetia, which had been part of the territory of Kavkas.
Durdzuk, who was the most eminent among the sons of Kavkas, went and settled in a gorge of the mountains and gave it his own name, Durdzuketi. He paid tribute to the king of the Khazars.
On that same campaign the king of the Khazars gave his paternal cousin (the son of his father's brother) part of the territory of Lekan, east of the Sea of Darubandi as far as the Lomeki river.
He also gave him captives from Ran and Movakan. He settled there, in what had been part of the territory of Lekan.
Khozonikh, who was the most eminent among the peoples of Lekan, went and settled in a gorge of the mountains. He built a city and gave it his own name, Khozanikheti.
Much time passed in this way, and all these peoples were tributaries of the Khazars.
After that the Persians, descendants of Nimrod, grew strong in the east. Among the descendants of Nimrod there appeared a hero
named Apridon (Faridun), "who bound Bevrasp, lord of serpents, with chains and tied him up on a mountain that no human can climb," as it is said.
This is what is written in the Life of the Persians: Aphridon ruled over the whole land of the Persians.
To some lands he sent eristavis, his officials, and some lands he made tributary.
He sent his own eristavi with a great army. His name was Ardam, a son of the kindred of Nimrod.
He came to Kartli and destroyed all the cities and fortresses of Kartli. He also slaughtered every Khazar he found in Kartli.
This eristavi Ardam built a city at the Sea Gate and named it Darubandi (Derbent), which is translated "he closed the gate."
He also walled the city of Mtskheta with stone and lime mortar. Until then there had been no stone-and-lime work in Kartli, and because of this they learned to build with stone and lime.
This same Ardam built a lime-mortar wall for the fortress of Armazi, and from there down to the Mtkvari. He walled the ridge of Armazi as far as the Mtkvari. Ardam was eristavi for many years.
When Aphridon divided the whole land among his three sons, the son to whom he gave Persia as his house also received Kartli as his share. That son's name was Iared.
After Ardam the eristavi, the other eristavis also died.
From then on the sons of Aphridon were preoccupied, because they began to fight one another. The two brothers killed Iared, their brother.
Then the Kartlosids found a favourable moment. They negotiated with the Ossetians and brought the Ossetians down. They found the Persian eristavi on the plain

outside, while he was [? hunting / amusing himself], and they killed him. The Ossetians and the Georgians wiped out every Persian they found, and the Georgians were freed. But Ran and Hereti remained with the Persians.
Many years after this the Persians grew strong again, and the king of the Persians, whose name was Kekapos, became great.
At that time there was a certain man in Leketi, a sorcerer of the kindred of Khozanikhizi [?]. Through his sorcery he blinded King Kekapos and his army,
and so Kekapos could not enter Leketi. He turned back, and only then were his eyes given light again. This Kekapos again made the Georgians tributary and went away.
Some years after this, news came that Moses had taken the Israelites across the sea and that they were being fed in the desert with manna.
Everyone was amazed, and all those pagans praised the God of the Israelites.
Some years after this, Kekapos, king of the Persians, became preoccupied, because he began a war with the Turks.
Then the Armenians and the Georgians found a favourable moment. They rebelled against the Persians, fortified their fortresses and cities, and all the peoples descended from Targamos united.
Some years after this, Kekapos, king of the Persians, sent his son, whose name was Pharaborot, with a great army against the Armenians, the Georgians and all the Targamosids.
All these Targamosids gathered together, went out to meet him and fought a battle in Adarbadagan. They put Pharaborot to flight and slaughtered his army.
A few years after this, the same Kekapos again sent out his grandson, the son of Shiosh the Blessed, who had been killed in Turkestan, as is written in the Book of the Life of the Persians.
This son of Shiosh, named Kaikhosro, set out. The Armenians and the Georgians could not stand against him, because his power was great.

He went through all of Armenia and Kartli, took everything captive, and plundered all the fortresses and cities. He left eristavis there, built a house of prayer of their religion in Adarbadagan, and went away.
Some years after this, King Kaikhosro was free of other affairs. He began to make war on the Turks, seeking vengeance for the blood of his father.
The Armenians and the Georgians found their opportunity. They rebelled against the Persians, killed the Persian governors, and became free.
At that same time Turks came who had fled from that same Kaikhosro. They crossed the Sea of Gurgan, went up along the Kura, and came to Mtskheta, twenty-eight households.
They negotiated with the head of Mtskheta and promised him help against the Persians. The head of Mtskheta made this known to all the Georgians.
They decided to make friends with these Turks, because they feared the Persians. So for the sake of their help they made friends with those exiled Turks and brought them into all the cities.
Most of them came and found a place in Mtskheta, on the western side, a deep place cut out among the rocks. They asked the head of the people of Mtskheta for that place.
He gave it, and they built on it and walled it strongly. That place was called Sarkine.
These Turks and the Georgians did as each other wished. They waited for the Persians to come, and they strengthened the fortresses and cities.

At that time, whenever any evildoer arrived from anywhere, whether a fugitive from Greece, from Assyria, or from Khazaria, the Georgians made friends with all of them for the sake of help against the Persians.
Much time passed in this way. Then King Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem captive, and Jews who fled from there came to Kartli. They asked
the head of the people of Mtskheta for land in return for tribute. He gave it and settled them on the Aragvi, at the spring called Zanavi.
The land that they held for tribute (kharki) is now called Kherki because of that tribute. Until then the language that the descendants of Kartlos spoke was Armenian.
But when these countless peoples gathered in Kartli, the Georgians also gave up the Armenian language, and the Georgian language was formed from all these peoples.
They held a religion more wicked than that of any other people.
In marriage they paid no regard to kinship. They ate every living creature. There were no graves: they ate the dead.
Some years after this, the son of the Persian king Vashtashab came up. His name was Spandiat-Rvali, the famous giant.
The Armenians and the Georgians could not stand against him. Instead they strengthened their fortresses and cities and waited for him to come.
But when he reached Adarbadagan, news came to the Persians that the Turks had killed his grandfather and that the Turks had entered Persia.
Then Spandiat abandoned the war against the Armenians and the Georgians and turned against the Turks to avenge the blood of his grandfather. So the Armenians and the Georgians became free.
Some years after this, the son of Spandiat became king in Persia. His name was Baram, and he is known as Ardashir.
He became greater than all the kings of the Persians. He conquered Babylon and Assyria and made the Greeks and the Romans pay him tribute.
The Georgians also paid tribute to him at that time. All these peoples were mixed together in Kartli in this way, and six languages were spoken in Kartli:
Armenian, Georgian, Khazar, Syriac, Hebrew, and Greek. All the kings of Kartli knew these languages, both men and women.
Chapter Three: The Coming of Alexander and the Kings of the Line of Parnavaz. This Alexander appeared in the land of Greece,
[?] the land called Macedon, son of Nectanebo the Egyptian, as his story is written in the book of the Greeks.
This Alexander conquered all the ends of the earth.
He came out from the west and went into the south. He came back by the north, crossed over the Caucasus and came to Kartli.
And he found that all the Kartvelians were the most wicked of all peoples in their customs.
For in marriage and fornication they paid no regard to kinship. They ate every living thing, and they ate the dead, like wild beasts and cattle. It is not fitting to tell of their conduct.
And when he saw these fierce pagan peoples, whom we call Bun-Turks and Kipchaks, dwelling all around the river Mtkvari,
Alexander was amazed at this, for no other peoples did such things. He wished to root them out of their cities,
but at that time he could not, for he found strong fortresses and mighty cities.
Again other peoples, Chaldeans, came out, and they too settled in Kartli.
After this Alexander grew strong and conquered the whole earth, and he came up into the land of Kartli.
And he found these strong fortified cities in Central Kartli: Tsunda; Khertvisi on the Mtkvari; Odzrkhe, which clings to the rock of Ghado; Tukharisi, on the river Speri,
which is called the Chorokhi; Urbnisi, Kaspi and Uplistsikhe; the great city of Mtskheta and its quarters, Sarkine, Tsikhe-Didi and Zanavi, the quarter of the Jews;
and Rustavi; and Samshvilde, the mother-fortress; and Mtveris-tsikhe, which is Khunani; and the cities of Kakheti.
In all these fortified cities he found men who fought fiercely.
And he divided his army and laid siege to all these fortified cities, and he himself encamped at Mtskheta.
And he stationed troops on this side and that, above and below, and he himself encamped on the Ksani, at the place called Nastakisi.
But he did not fight against Mtveris-tsikhe and Tukharisi, for he would not have been able to take them.
The other fortresses and cities he took in six months. But the people of Sarkine, who were among the Bun-Turks, insulted the king.
Alexander grew angry. He no longer wished to make peace and would not accept their pleas. He said to them: "Since you have insulted me, this is your reward: I will kill you all."
And he surrounded the city of Sarkine, and not a single man could escape from anywhere. The people of Sarkine were hard pressed, for he fought against them for eleven months.
They began secretly to cut into the rock, and they bored through that rock, which was soft and easy to pierce.
And the people of Sarkine passed out through that hole by night and fled into the Caucasus, and they left the city empty.
Alexander conquered all of Kartli. He slaughtered all those mixed peoples living in Kartli, and he slaughtered and took captive those foreign peoples,
and the women and the children [?] under fifteen years of age. He spared the peoples descended from Kartlos, and he set over them as patrician a man named Azon,
son of Iaredos, his kinsman from the land of Macedon. And he gave him a hundred thousand men from the land of Rome which is called Protatos.
These Phrotatosians were strong and brave men, and they had been oppressing the land of the Romans.
And he brought them to Kartli and gave them to Azon the patrician. And he left Azon in Kartli as eristavi (governor), and those troops with him, to hold Kartli.
And Alexander commanded Azon that they should honour the sun and the moon and the five stars, and serve the invisible God, the Creator of all.
For at that time there was no prophet and no teacher of the true faith
who might teach and reprove; rather, Alexander himself devised this religion, and during his reign he laid down this religion for every land. And Alexander departed.
But this Azon tore down the walls of the city of Mtskheta to their foundations, and left standing the four fortresses that stood at the entrance of Kartli:
the chief fortress, which is Armazi; and one fortress at the end of the spur of Armazi; and one above Mtskheta;
the fourth fortress to the west of Mtskheta, on the Mtkvari (Kura). And he strengthened these and filled them with troops.
And he tore down the walls of all the cities of Kartli, and took possession of all the borders of Kartli, from Hereti and the Berduji river as far as the sea of Speri.
And in addition to Kartli he also took possession of Egrisi, and made the Ossetians, the Leks, and the Khazars tributaries.
And when Alexander went to Egypt, he built the city of Alexandria, and within twelve years he went around the whole world; within twelve years he had seized all the ends of the earth.
And in the fourteenth year he died, it is said, in Alexandria, that great and unequalled sovereign. And as he was dying,
while he was still alive, he released all the princes who had been captured and enslaved by him.
And they went each to his own land, as had been commanded.
Then he brought four men of his own kin, whose names were Antiochus, Romus, Byzantius, and Plato.
And he gave Asurastan (Syria) and Armenia to Antiochus, and assigned to him the eastern region. And he built a city named after himself, Antioch.
And to Romus he gave Thrimikos [?], and assigned him the western region. And he built the city of Rome.
And to Byzantius he gave Greece and Kartli, and assigned him the northern region.
And he wrote a letter of testament to Azon the patrician, eristavi of Kartli, that he should serve Byzantius.
And he (Byzantius) built the city of Byzantium, which is now called Constantinople. And he left Plato in Alexandria. And Alexander died.
But this Azon abandoned the religion given by Alexander and began to serve idols, and he made two silver idols, Gatsi and Gaim.
And he was subject to Byzantius, king of Greece.
He was a harsh and bloodthirsty man, and he decreed this and commanded his troops: "Any Georgian whom you find with a weapon, kill him."
And those Romans did this to the Georgians, and whenever any Georgian appeared who was handsome and full-grown, they would kill him.
And there was great affliction upon the Georgian people. And this Azon was bloodthirsty toward those Romans as well, and many of them were slaughtered.
The Life of Parnavaz, who was the first king of Kartli, of the line of Kartlos. At that time there was a young man in the city of Mtskheta whose name was Parnavaz.
This Parnavaz was a Kartlian on his father's side, a kinsman of Uplos son of Mtskhetos, and on his mother's side a Persian from Ispahan.
He was the nephew of Samara, who had been the chief elder (mamasakhlisi) of Mtskheta at the time when Alexander came.
This Samara and his brother, the father of Parnavaz, had been killed by Alexander.
But Parnavaz's mother had taken Parnavaz, a child of three years, and fled to the Caucasus. He was brought up there, and then he had come to Mtskheta, the land of his fathers.
This Parnavaz was a wise man, a bold horseman and a skilled hunter. But he hid his excellence out of fear of Azon.
Through his hunting, however, he became known to Azon, and Azon grew fond of him because of his hunting.
His mother begged Parnavaz: "My son, beware of Azon, and do not show any of your excellence, or they may kill you."
And fear and trembling were upon him. As the fear of Azon grew upon them, his mother said to Parnavaz:
"My son, leave the dwelling of your fathers and take me to my homeland, Ispahan, to my brothers, and save yourself alive from the hand of Azon."
And they settled on this plan, to go to Ispahan. It was hard for Parnavaz to leave the dwelling of his fathers, but because of his great fear he resolved to go.
Then Parnavaz saw a dream: he was in an empty house, and he wanted to get out but could not.
Then a ray of the sun came in through his window and wrapped itself around his waist, and it drew him out and led him through the window.
When he had gone out into the field, he saw the sun hanging low. He stretched out his hand, wiped the dew from the face of the sun, and anointed his own face with it.
Parnavaz woke up and was amazed, and he said: "This is the meaning of that dream: I shall go to Ispahan, and there I shall be granted good fortune."
That same day Parnavaz went out and hunted alone, and he chased deer on the plain of Dighomi. The deer fled into the rocky ravines of Tbilisi.
Parnavaz pursued them, shot an arrow and hit a deer. The deer went a little way and fell at the foot of a cliff.
Parnavaz came up to the deer. The day had passed into evening, and he sat down beside the deer, intending to spend the night there and leave in the morning.
At the foot of that cliff there was a cave, whose entrance had been walled up with stones long ago, and with age the masonry had begun to crumble.
Then a heavy rain poured down. Parnavaz took out his axe and broke open the entrance of the cave, so that there
inside he might take shelter from the rain, and he went into the cave. And there inside he saw an immeasurable treasure: gold and silver, and countless vessels of gold and silver.
Then Parnavaz was astonished and filled with joy. He remembered the dream, and he closed up the entrance of the cave again just as it had been.
And he quickly came away and told his mother and his two sisters.
That same night the three of them went out with leather sacks and vessels, and began to carry out the treasure and bury it wherever was convenient for them.
And each time dawn was breaking, they would wall up the entrance of the cave again in the same way.
And so they gathered up that treasure over five nights and stored it away [?] in their secure place. Then Pharnavaz sent his servant to Kuji and said:
"I am a kinsman of Uplos, son of Mtskhetos, and the nephew of Samara the mamasakhlisi, and I have a very great treasure with me.
Now, if you wish, I will come to you with that treasure, and let us be brothers and use that treasure together, the two of us.
Let us show ourselves as enemies of Azon the eristavi, and our fortune will give us a good victory." Then Kuji rejoiced with great joy and said:
"Arise and come to me, and do not begrudge your treasure. With your treasure I will multiply your troops until we come out openly as Azon's enemies.
Then all the Georgians who have been slaughtered and oppressed [?] by him will rejoice.
And I think that some of the Romans too will join us, for countless numbers of them too have been slaughtered by Azon."
Then Pharnavaz went away secretly and joyfully. He took with him as much of that treasure as he could, and his mother and his sisters went with him too.
And he came to Kuji, and Kuji said to him: "You are a child of the chiefs of Kartli, and lordship over me belongs to you. Now do not begrudge your treasure, so that we may multiply our troops;
and if victory is given to us, you are our lord and I am your servant."

Then they joined forces and negotiated with the Ossetians and the Leks. The Ossetians and the Leks rejoiced, for they did not like paying tribute to Azon. So they followed them, and their troops grew in number.
Countless troops gathered from Egrisi, and they marched against Azon. Azon called up his own troops and gathered them.
Then a thousand chosen horsemen from among the Romans, who had suffered harm from Azon, broke away from Azon and came before Pharnavaz.
Then all the Georgians broke away from Azon. As for the troops that remained with Azon, he could no longer trust them, for he had done evil to everyone.
Azon left and went to Klarjeti, and he fortified himself in the strongholds of Klarjeti.
Pharnavaz came to Mtskheta and seized the four fortresses of Mtskheta. Within that same year he seized all of Kartli except Klarjeti.
This Pharnavaz sent envoys to Antiochus, king of Asurastan, and sent him very great gifts.
He promised to serve him and asked him for help against the Greeks.
Antiochus accepted his gifts, called him his son, and sent him a crown. He also ordered the eristavis of Armenia to help Pharnavaz.
In the second year Azon gathered troops from Greece, grew very strong, and marched against Pharnavaz.
By then the horsemen of Kartli on Pharnavaz's side had grown in number. He called them up, and he summoned Kuji and the Ossetians.
All of these assembled, and the eristavis of Antiochus came from Armenia and joined them.
Pharnavaz gathered all of these together and went to meet Azon near the ruined city of Artaani, which was then called the City of the Kajis, and which is Huri.
They drew up their battle lines there, and a very great battle took place. Countless men fell on both sides, but the Greeks were defeated by Pharnavaz.
Their camp fled, and Azon was killed. Countless of his troops were slaughtered or taken captive.
Parnavaz went and plundered the border of Greece, Andzianddzora [?], and returned by way of Ekeletsi.
He came to Klarjeti and conquered Klarjeti, and came back to Mtskheta with great joy.
Azon's treasure was also added to his wealth, and his wealth became immense.
But the land below the Egris River remained with the Greeks, because the inhabitants of that place did not want to break away from the Greeks.
Then Parnavaz gave his sister in marriage to the king of the Ossetians, and he gave his second sister in marriage to Kuji.
He gave Kuji the land between the Egris River and the Rioni, from the sea to the mountains, which contains Egrisi and Svaneti, and he confirmed him there as eristavi (duke).
Kuji built the fortress of Tsikhe-Goji. Then Parnavaz became free from fear of all his enemies, and he became king over all Kartli and Egrisi.
He increased the number of all the Kartlosian horsemen, and he appointed eight eristavis and a spaspeti (commander-in-chief).
He sent one as eristavi of Margvi, and gave him the land from the Little Mountain, which is Likhi, as far as the border of Egrisi, above the Rioni.
This same Parnavaz built two fortresses, Shorapani and Dimna.
He sent the second as eristavi of Kakheti, and gave him the land from the Aragvi as far as Hereti, which is Kakheti and Kukheti.
He sent the third as eristavi of Khunani, and gave him the land from the Berduji River as far as Tbilisi and Gachiani, which is Gardabani.
He sent the fourth as eristavi of Samshvilde, and gave him the land from the Skvireti River as far as the mountain, which is Tashiri and Abotsi.
He sent the fifth as eristavi of Tsunda, and gave him the land from Panvari as far as the source of the Mtkvari, which is Javakheti, Kola and Artani.
He sent the sixth as eristavi of Odzrkhe, and gave him the land from Tasiskari as far as Arsiani, and from the source of the Nosti to the sea, which is Samtskhe and Ajara.
He sent the seventh as eristavi of Klarjeti, and gave him the land from Arsiani to the sea. The eighth, Kuji, was eristavi of Egrisi.
He appointed one as spaspeti, and gave him the land from Tbilisi and the Aragvi as far as Tasiskari and Panvari, which is Inner Kartli (Shida Kartli). This spaspeti was
next in rank before the king, and he governed with authority over all the eristavis.
Under these eristavis, in their various districts, he appointed spasalars (commanders) and commanders of a thousand, and royal and ducal tribute came from all of them.
In this way Parnavaz arranged all of this in imitation of the kingdom of the Persians. He took a wife from the Durdzuks, of the race of Kavkas.
This Parnavaz fortified the city of Mtskheta strongly, and he rebuilt all the cities and fortresses of Kartli that Alexander had laid waste.
The Greeks could no longer take revenge on him, because they were occupied with war against the Romans.
This same Parnavaz made a great idol in his own name. This is Armazi, for in Persian Parnavaz was called Armaz.
He set up the idol Armazi at the head of Kartli, and from then on the place was called Armazi because of that idol.
He held a great festival for the idol he had set up. He became king at the age of twenty-seven, and he reigned for sixty-five years in prosperity.
And he served Antiochus, king of Assyria. And all his days, from the time he took the throne, he spent in peace, and he built up Kartli and filled it with people.
He would spend the spring and autumn months in Mtskheta, the royal city, and the winter months in Gachiani, and the summer months in Tsunda.
And from time to time he would go to Egrisi and Klarjeti, and visit the Megrelians and the Klarjians, and set in order every matter that had fallen into disorder.
Now those thousand Roman horsemen who had come over to Parnavaz from Azon, whom we mentioned above, he distributed among the valleys and lands,
and he treated them well, for they had been brave in that battle against Azon. And he called them by the name aznauri (nobles).
And after Alexander had departed, they no longer ate human beings, except those whom they offered to the idol as a sacrifice.
There was rest and joy over all Kartli because of the reign of Parnavaz, and everyone said this:
"We give thanks to our fortune, for it has given us a king from the race of our fathers, and has lifted from us the tribute and the oppression of foreign peoples."
And Parnavaz accomplished all this by wisdom and virtue, by courage and wealth.
A son was born to him, and he named him Saurmag. And this Parnavaz was the first king in Kartli from the race of Kartlos.
He spread the Georgian language, and no other language was spoken any longer in Kartli except Georgian.
And he created Georgian writing. And Parnavaz died, and they buried him before the idol Armazi.
The second king, Saurmag. And in his place his son Saurmag became king. At that time the eristavis (dukes) of Kartli took counsel together and said:
"It is not good for us to serve one of our own kin. Rather, let us unite and kill Saurmag, and be our own masters,
as we were before, and pay tribute to whoever shows himself the victor. For by being this way we will have more rest."
They settled on the plan to kill Saurmag. But Saurmag learned of it, and he left secretly and fled.
He took his mother with him and went to the land of the Durdzuks, to his mother's brothers. Then those Roman aznauri set out and also came to Durdzuketi, and said to Saurmag:
"Your father did us great good. Therefore we stand firm in our loyalty to you."
Then Saurmag sent word to the king of the Ossetians, his father's sister's son, and asked for help.
And the king gladly went to help him, and Saurmag also gathered the Durdzuks and marched against the Georgians.
And no one was able to stand against him. And he took Kartli and slew those who had rebelled against him.
Some he pardoned. But he humbled the Kartlosids and raised the aznauri to distinction, and he made the Durdzuks, the kinsmen of Kavkas, numerous.
For during the Khazar raids they had all remained unharmed in peace because their land was so well fortified, and Durdzuketi could no longer hold them all.
Then this Saurmag brought away half of all of them, of the peoples descended from Kavkas, and some of them he raised to distinction,
and others he settled in the mountain country, from Didoeti as far as Egrisi, which is Svaneti. And he kept these as his own trusted people, being his kin on his mother's side.
And Saurmag sat as king in Mtskheta. And he strengthened all the fortresses of Mtskheta and Kartli.
And he made two idols, Ainina and Danana, and set them up on the road to Mtskheta.
And he served the king of Assyria. And he took a Persian wife, the daughter of the eristavi (governor) of Bardav.
And he had two daughters by her, but no son was born to him. Then he brought from Persia a descendant of Nimrod,
from his wife's kin, the son of her mother's sister, and he adopted him as his son. His name was Mirvan.

And he gave him his daughter as wife, together with the city of Gachiani and the eristavate (governorship) of Samshvilde. And he gave his other daughter to the son of Kuji, his own father's sister's son.
Saurmag reigned happily for many years. And Saurmag died, and his adopted son Mirvan became king in his place.
The third king, Mirvan. This Mirvan, of the line of Nimrod, was perfect in stature, handsome, strong, brave and noble.
During his reign the Durdzuks forgot their affection for Parnavaz and Saurmag; and they came down,
those who lived in Durdzuketi, and joined with the Caucasians who lived in Chartaleti, and plundered Kakheti and Bazaleti.
Then King Mirvan summoned all the eristavis of Kartli and gathered all the troops, cavalry and infantry.
And all the Caucasians who had been brought down by King Saurmag remained faithful in their obedience to Mirvan, except those of Chartali.
He gathered all these and set out for Durdzuketi. The Durdzuks gathered and took their stand on the fortifications on the road of the pass.
Then Mirvan dismounted from his horse, went to his foot soldiers, and led the way at the head of the infantry, placing the cavalry behind them.
And he came against the gates like a tiger in ferocity, like a leopard in courage, like a lion in roaring. A fierce battle took place between them.
But the swords of the Durdzuks could not cut Mirvan, as though he were smooth rock, and he stood unmoved like a strong tower. And the fighting between them went on for a long time.
The Georgians pressed on from behind, slaughtered them and took captives. And Mirvan entered Durdzuketi and laid waste Durdzuketi and Chartali.
And he closed the gates with stone and lime and gave them the name Darubal. And Mirvan settled in Mtskheta and reigned in comfort and without fear.
He was a man who gave good things generously, and all the inhabitants of Kartli loved him. And he served the king of the Assyrians.
At this time the kingship of Antiochus in Babylon passed away. And at that time a man named Arshak became king in Armenia.
Mirvan entered into an alliance with Arshak and gave his daughter to Arshak's son, Arshak. And Mirvan died, and his son Parnajom became king in his place.
The fourth king, Parnajom, of the line of Nimrod. This King Parnajom added to the building of all the fortresses and cities, and he built the fortress of Zadeni,
and he made an idol named Zaden and set it up at Zadeni. And he began to build in Kakheti the city of Nelkari, which is Nekresi.
After this he came to love the religion of the Persians, the worship of fire, and he brought fire-worshippers and magi from Persia,
and settled them in Mtskheta, at the place which is now called Mogvta ("of the Magi"), and he began openly to revile the idols.
For this reason the inhabitants of Kartli came to hate him, for they had great devotion to the idols.
Then most of the eristavis of Kartli conspired together, and they sent an envoy to the king of the Armenians and said:
"Our king has transgressed the religion of our fathers; he no longer serves the gods who rule Kartli. He has adopted his father's religion and abandoned his mother's religion.
Now he is no longer worthy to be our king. Give us your son Arshak, whose wife is of the lineage of the Parnavazians, our kings.
Help us with your force, and we will drive out Parnajom, who brought in the new religion, and let your son Arshak be our king and his wife, a child of our kings, be our queen."
Then this plan pleased the king of the Armenians. He sent their envoy back with a favourable answer and said to them:
"If you truly, with pure hearts, want my son as your king, then all of you eristavis give me hostages, and I will give you my son as your king, and I will fill you with every kind of gift."
Then most of the eristavis of Kartli gave hostages and openly declared their revolt against Parnajom.
Then the king of the Armenians set out for Kartli with all his forces.
But King Parnajom called on the Persians and brought powerful Persian forces, and he also gathered those Georgians who had remained loyal to him.
The rebel eristavis of Kartli went to meet the king of the Armenians at Tashir, and a multitude of Armenians and Georgians assembled there. And Parnajom went to meet them there at Tashir.
A fierce battle took place between them, and countless men fell on both sides, for Parnajom was defeated by the Armenians and the Georgians. Parnajom was killed and his army was destroyed.
But Parnajom's son Mirvan, a child of one year, was taken away by his foster-father, who fled to Persia. And the king of the Armenians gave them his son Arshak.
The fifth king, Arshak, of the Arsacids. Arshak sat as king and took possession of all Kartli. He ruled as he pleased and strengthened all the fortresses of Kartli.
Above all he reinforced the walls in Javakheti, at the city of Tsunda. Arshak died, and his son Artag became king.
The sixth king, Artag, of the Arsacids. This king Artag reigned only two years.
In the second year of his reign the eristavis of the Persians came with a great army to avenge the blood of Parnajom and of the Persian troops who had been slain together with Parnajom.
Artag, king of the Georgians, could not stand against them, for the might of the Persians was great, but he fortified the fortresses and the cities.
The Persians overran all Kartli and laid waste the open country, but they could not take any of the fortresses or cities, and they departed. Artag died, and his son Bartom sat in his place.
The seventh king, Bartom, of the Arsacids. This king Bartom strengthened the walls of Mtskheta and all the fortifications of Kartli.
Meanwhile the Persians raised Parnajom's son Mirvan, whom his foster-father, mentioned above, had carried away at the time of Parnajom's death. This Mirvan
was a good man, brave and a skilled horseman, and he was tested many times in battle against the Turks and the Arabs.
This Mirvan gathered powerful forces in Persia and set out for Kartli. He sent an envoy to the eristavis of Kartli and said to them:
"Remember the love of my father's father, Mirvan, and his kindness toward you.
Even though my father brought a foreign religion among you, you also received good from him.
"My father was killed justly, because he did not keep the law of your fathers well. So now let there be no grief or fear in your hearts over my father's death,
for fathers kill their sons and brothers kill their brothers for abandoning the law, and the blood of those killed for abandoning the law is not avenged.
I am a son of your kings, the Parnavazids. Although I was raised among the Persians, I hold to the law of your fathers,
and I trust in the gods who rule Kartli. With hope in them I have set out to claim my patrimony. Now expect glory and good things from me."
But the eristavis of Kartli did not accept Mirvan's command. Instead, they all went before King Bartom.
But a few Georgians, who were not of the nobility, went and joined Mirvan.
King Bartom gathered all the troops of Kartli, brought in forces from Armenia, and went out to meet him at Khunani. He kept the city of Khunani at his rear.
Mirvan came and halted at the river Berduji. They began to fight, and champions came forward there from both sides.
For one month the champions fought every day. Sometimes those won, and sometimes these won.
During that one month Mirvan himself killed thirteen champions of the Georgians and Armenians.
No one among the Georgians and Armenians appeared who could defeat Mirvan. King Bartom himself could not fight him either, because Bartom did not have a giant's strength.
Then King Bartom drew up his troops and advanced with his whole army against Mirvan, and Mirvan came from his side to meet him with his whole army.
A fierce battle took place between them, and countless men fell on both sides. The Armenians and Georgians were defeated by the Persians, and they killed Bartom, king of the Georgians.
This King Bartom had no son, only one daughter. During his lifetime he had brought from Egrisi a grandson of Kuji named Kartam,
who was of Parnavazid descent through Kuji's wife, who was Parnavaz's sister, and through his own mother, Saurmag's daughter, who was the wife of Kuji's son.
King Bartom had given his daughter in marriage to this Kartam from Egrisi and had adopted him as his son.
Bartom had done this to please the Georgians, because the Georgians had great affection for the Parnavazids,
and they did not want a king from any other lineage that had no Parnavazid descent.
This Kartam, King Bartom's adopted son, was killed together with Bartom in that same battle.
His wife, Bartom's daughter, was left [?helpless/pregnant]. She fled to Armenia, and there she gave birth to a boy and named him Aderki, and he was raised there.
After Mirvan killed Bartom, he entered Kartli and took control of
all of Kartli. To the eristavis of Kartli who were still holding out in fortresses and strongholds he gave an oath and a promise, and he brought them all out.
He forcibly brought Bartom's wife out of Samshvilde and married her. She was also a descendant of the Arsacids. He settled in Mtskheta.
The eighth king. Mirvan reigned in ease for a short time and died. His son Arshak took the throne in his place.
The ninth king, Arshak II, son of Mirvan, a Nimrodid. This King Arshak was an Arsacid on his mother's side, and a Nimrodid and a Parnavazid on his father's side.
This Arshak improved Nelkar, a city of Kakheti, which is Nekresi, and he strengthened the fortifications of Uplistsikhe.
He was mighty in strength, huge, a giant. Now this Aderki, son of Kartam and grandson through his daughter of King Bartom, whom we mentioned above, was raised in Armenia.
He was a handsome man, tall in body, a giant. He had been tested many times in battle against the Armenians and the Assyrians, he had killed many champions, and he had become famous.
This Aderki asked the king of the Armenians for troops, and the king gave them to him. He set out against Arshak, king of the Georgians, his mother's brother.
But Arshak gathered all the eristavis of Kartli, brought in forces from Persia, and went out to meet him.
The two armies met at Trialeti and camped close to each other.
Arshak challenged Aderki to single combat. Aderki gladly armed himself in splendid armor, mounted his steed, and said to his troops:
"Guard my back for me, and do not be afraid." Arshak likewise armed himself and rode out between the battle lines.
Both of them shouted with fierce voices and charged at each other. Both began striking with spears, but neither could pierce the other's armor.
As the fight dragged on, their spears broke. They drew their maces and began fighting with maces.
Whenever they struck the mace against each other's armor, the sound was like the sound of a smith's hammer striking the anvil,
and the sound of their shouting was like thunder. Even then they could not overcome each other. They grew tired and drew back, one to each side.
Night fell on that day and both of them rested. In the morning they came out again, took up their bows, and began charging and shooting at each other.
Aderki shot an arrow into Arshak's chest, and the strength of his armor could no longer protect him. The arrow came out through his back, and Arshak fell from his horse.
Aderki quickly turned back, went to the Armenian troops, and said to them:
"I adjure you by your gods: do not draw your swords against the Georgians, for they are my ancestral people.
And now I am their king, through your strength and help." The Armenians listened to his plea and stayed where they were.
Aderki turned and came close to the Georgian troops, and called out in a loud voice: "I am the son of your kings, and my fate has given the kingship
to me. Now receive from me good things and joy. See, I will no longer let the Armenian troops loose on you."
Then the Georgians answered: "You have shown yourself the best among all the descendants of Parnavaz. Since this king of ours has died, you are now our king.
We thank our fate, for in place of this king of ours we have been given a son of our own kings, a giant and a man of renown."
All the Georgians dismounted, fell on their faces, and bowed down to Aderki.
The Armenians, the Georgians, and the Persians of Ran came together in peace. The Georgians brought Arshak's crown, placed it on Aderki, and led him in.
The tenth king: Aderki, son of Bartom, an Arsacid. This Aderki took control of the whole land of Kartli and Egrisi.
The king of the Armenians gave him his daughter as a wife. He took the throne in Mtskheta and reigned well. He became king at thirty years of age and reigned fifty-seven years.
In the very first year of his reign our Lord Jesus Christ was born, in Bethlehem of Judea.
Magi came to him to offer gifts. When those magi entered Jerusalem, news reached Mtskheta that "the Persians have taken Jerusalem captive."
There was mourning and weeping among the Jews who were in Mtskheta. Then in the second year another report came that "those Persians
did not come to Jerusalem to take it captive. Instead, they had gifts for a certain child who had been born." And the Jews of Mtskheta rejoiced.
After this, when thirty years had passed, envoys of the Jews came from Jerusalem to the Jews of Mtskheta with this message:
"He for whom the magi came and offered gifts has grown up, and he calls himself the Son of God.
Now they have sent us as envoys to all the Jews, so that those learned in the Law may come, and we may examine him and pass judgement on him.
So now let those learned in the Law come from among you there too, so that we may keep the law of our fathers unchanged and uphold it, and fulfil the commandment of Moses,
so that the simpler people of our faith are not led astray by this new law that he preaches to us. And let us take vengeance on him through his death as well."
So Elioz, an old man, went. He had a mother from the tribe of Eli the priest, and also a sister. As he was leaving, his mother pleaded with her son, saying:
"Go then, beloved child, in answer to the summons of the ruler and the order of the Law. But keep only this, which I command you:
do not let your mind join in their evil plan, and do not in any way take part in shedding his blood. No, my son,
I beg you, no! For know without doubt that he is the word of the prophets, which they proclaimed beforehand from the very beginning."
Elioz of Mtskheta and Longinoz of Karsani went from here. There they happened to be present at the crucifixion of the Lord, and they brought the Lord's robe back from there,
Elioz of Mtskheta and Longinoz of Karsani, as this is plainly written in The Conversion of Kartli.
When they were nailing the Lord to the cross in Jerusalem, at the very moment the hammer struck the nails, Elioz's mother heard the sound in Mtskheta.
She cried out with a terrible shriek and said: "Farewell, kingdom of Israel, for in your folly you have killed,
you wretched and lost ones, the Lord and Saviour of all, and in your wickedness you have become murderers of your Creator.
Woe to you, wretched ones! Who could ever find mourning great enough for what you deserve?
But woe even more to me, for before my death my ears have heard the sound of every sorrow."
And immediately, at these words, the woman died, in great and indescribable grief and mourning.
When the godless Jews cast lots for the Lord's robe at his crucifixion, the providence of God gave it to the Jews of Mtskheta.
Elioz and Longinoz came from Jerusalem, and he brought back that holy robe.
When Elioz brought it to Mtskheta, his sister at once came out to meet him, lamenting and weeping terribly, soaked with tears, and she threw her arms around the neck of her beloved brother.
When she saw the tunic of our Saviour, more desirable than every desirable thing, she at once pressed it to her breast with longing and love,
and at that very moment the blessed woman gave up her spirit, for three reasons: first, because of the death and Passion of the Lord;
second, because her brother had taken part in the blood of the Lord; and third, because she remembered her mother's sorrowful death as well.
Since all these sorrows came upon her together, she was overcome in her human nature, and death took her, broken by her many sorrows.
Then this great and wonderful event was heard of throughout the whole city of Mtskheta, and when it became known
to the king, to all the princes and to all the people, they were all amazed together at this awesome event.
When King Aderki saw the holy tunic, it pleased him greatly because of its beauty, and he wanted to put that garment on his own defiled body.
But because of the miracle and what had caused it, he no longer wished to take it from the dead woman's breast.
Elioz buried his sister with a blessed burial. As she held the tunic on her breast, so he buried them together.
The holy tunic remained holy and still abides holy as it was before, as is clearly written in the Conversion of Kartli.
After the Ascension of the Lord, when the apostles cast lots, the land of Georgia fell by lot to the all-holy Mother of God to convert.
Her Son, our Lord, appeared to her in a vision and said: "O my mother, through your intercession for them, I will not neglect that [?] people above all nations.
Send Andrew the First-Called to the portion that has fallen to you, and send with him your image, which will be formed by placing it on your face.
In your place your image will remain as their guardian for all ages." Then the all-holy one said to the apostle Andrew:
"My son Andrew, it grieves my soul greatly that the name of my Son has not been preached in the land that is my portion.
When I set out to preach my Son in the land that fell to me by lot, my good Son and God appeared to me
and commanded that you should go and carry my image and that of my good Son to the land that fell to my lot,
so that I may be the guide of their life, stretch out my hand and help them, and so that none of their enemies may overpower them."

The apostle said to her: "All-holy one, may the will of your good Son and your own be done at all times." Then the all-holy one asked for a wooden board, washed her face and placed the board on her face.
And an image was formed of her carrying in her bosom the incarnate child, the all-good Word of God,
which is now seen by all as the icon of the all-holy Mother of God of Atskuri.
She gave it to the apostle Andrew and said: "May the grace and help of the Lord born of me be your helper
wherever you go. I too am a helper in your preaching, and I will greatly help the portion that has fallen to me."
Then the apostle fell to the ground and gave thanks to the all-holy one with tears. He went out from there with joy and set out to preach the Gospel.
This King Aderki added to the fortifications of Kartli, its cities and fortresses. He also strengthened the walls of the city of Mtskheta further, on both this side and the far side of the river.
During the reign of this same Aderki, two of the twelve holy apostles, Andrew and Simon the Canaanite, came to Abkhazia and Egrisi.
The holy Simon the Canaanite died there, in the city of Nikopsia, on the border of the Greeks. Andrew converted the Megrelians and set off by the road of Klarjeti.
Andrew came to the city of Trebizond, which is a district of the Megrelians. He stayed there a short time and saw the beastlike foolishness of the inhabitants of that city.
He left that place and entered the land of Kartli called Great Adjara, and he began to preach the gospel.
The people were more foolish than beasts. They did not know God the Creator, and they practised every abominable and unclean custom, things that are improper even to speak of.

He endured many hardships and trials at the hands of the unbelievers. With the help of God and of the holy icon he bore them all with thanksgiving, until he had converted all of them and brought them to the faith.
In the place where he set down the icon of the all-holy Mother of God, a large and very beautiful spring burst forth, and it still flows without ceasing to this day.
All the inhabitants of that land gathered from every side, and he baptized them all in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
He appointed priests and deacons and set down for them the rule and bounds of the faith. They built a beautiful church in the name of the all-holy Mother of God.
When the holy apostle wished to leave that place, they begged him and would not let him go, but said to him:
"If you are leaving, leave that icon of the all-holy Mother of God here with us, as our hope and protector."
The holy apostle Andrew made a wooden panel of the same size and laid it on top of the icon.
Immediately the exact likeness of that icon was imprinted on the panel, unchanged, and he gave it to them.
They received it with joy and placed it with honour in their church, where it remains to this very day.
They bade the holy apostle farewell in peace, took leave of him tenderly, kissed him and sent him on his way.
He set out and crossed the mountain called Rkinis-Jvari ("Iron Cross"). It is said that the cross there was erected by the blessed Andrew himself.
When he had gone down the gorge of Odzrakhe and come to the borders of Samtskhe, he stopped for the night in a village called Zaden-gora.
The apostle looked around and saw that the people of that place were sacrificing to deaf idols. The apostle prayed before the holy icon,
and all those idols fell down and were shattered.
The holy apostle set out again and reached Atskveri, which was formerly called Sosangeti, with Sakrisi facing it.
He stopped at a place where there was an idol temple, now called Dzveli-Eklesia ("Old Church"). In that temple the people worshipped their idols.
At that time a certain woman, a widow in mourning, was the ruler there. She had only one son, and all her hope rested on him. At that very time he had died.

There was great lamentation and weeping and much commotion. That night, from the fortress, they saw a great light where the icon of the all-holy one lay, and they were greatly amazed and wondered who these people were.
When day broke, they quickly sent men to see who they were, or what this was.
When those men saw the holy apostle and the icon of the All-Holy, they quickly went and told the widowed woman: "Strange
men of some kind are here, and they preach a strange God as Creator and Maker, and as the giver of life
to people and the raiser of the dead. They have a beautiful icon, and they honor it."
When the woman heard this word about the raising of the dead, she was amazed, and her heart was comforted a little.
She sent her servants to call the apostle. When he came, the woman said to him: "Who are you?
Where do you come from? And what is this strange teaching of yours that you speak of? For such an account has never been heard anywhere."
The holy apostle answered and said to her: "I come from the holy city of Jerusalem, where the feet of the Lord stood, from Golgotha and Bethlehem, places that imitate the heavens.
I am a servant and apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, who raises the dead in an instant. I preach him as God and Lord and Ruler of all created things.
Whoever believes in him and is baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit will be given whatever he asks for in faith, and will be healed of every disease."
When the woman heard this, she fell to the ground and said to the apostle in tears: "Have mercy on my widowhood and my wretchedness.
Since you are a servant of the one who raises the dead, pray to your God and grant life to this son of mine. Then I will obey whatever you command me, and I will not be disobedient to you,
if I see my son raised up. For he is the only one I have, and I have no other." The holy apostle answered and said to her:
"If you believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the true God, who is preached by us, then whatever you ask for in faith will all be given to you by him."
When the woman heard this, she was filled with joy and said to the apostle in tears:
"O servant of the true God, I truly believe in and confess Jesus Christ, whom you preach. But help my unbelief."
Then the apostle sent out all the people and the mourners, and left no one there except the widow and a few of her own household.
He took in his hands the icon of the All-Holy Mother of God and laid it on the bier where the boy was lying.
He began to pray and make supplication to God with his hands raised.
After the prayer he took the boy by the hand and raised him up as if from sleep, and gave him to his mother.
When everyone saw this strange miracle, they were greatly amazed and could not say anything.
When the woman saw her son brought back to life, she rose up with joy and fell at the apostle's feet.
In tears she bowed down to him and gave thanks. She believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, and the woman was baptized together with her son and her whole household.
She quickly sent out her servants and dispatched letters to the princes of Samtskhe, writing to them as follows:
"Behold, brothers, I, a widow, announce to you great joy for all peoples.
"A certain man has come from a foreign land, who preaches a strange god, and he has an icon from heaven, which raised my dead son."
"So come quickly now, so that we may pick out the better way and law, and learn what is right."
When the Meskhians heard this wonderful news, they quickly gathered from every side, and the crowd of people became very great, until the plain of Sakrisi was filled.
And everyone was amazed when they saw the widow's son risen from the dead.
Now in that city there was an idol shrine, in which their foul gods, Artemis and Apollo, were served.
When those priests of falsehood saw this, they were filled with envy and began to dispute with the apostle and oppose him. Among the people as well, some said:
"We ought to worship the one who performed such a miracle," while others said: "Apollo and Artemis are great gods."
And there was dispute and uproar among them, until they confirmed the following course and decision, with all the people as witnesses.
And he said: "Open the door of that idol temple of yours, and let us place this icon in the middle of your idols, and let both of us together seal the door,
"and set guards, and pray to your gods tonight.
"And we will pray to Jesus Christ, our true God, and at dawn we shall see:
"if your god prevails, then it will be right to worship him; but if our God prevails, let us all worship him."
And they settled it this way. They placed the icon of the all-holy Mother of God in the middle of their idols and sealed the door,
and they set guards, and those priests of falsehood began to pray. And the saint prayed to Christ, our true God.
When dawn came and they opened the door of the idol temple, they saw all their idols thrown down on the ground and smashed like dust.
But the icon of the all-holy Mother of God shone like the sun, with glory and honour.
Then those idol priests were filled with shame, and they begged the apostle for forgiveness for their ignorance.
And all the people raised a voice of thanksgiving and said: "Great is the God of the Christians, whom the apostle Andrew preaches."
And all of them believed in our Lord Jesus Christ, and with joy they were all baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
And there was great joy that day among all the people, and they glorified God, who had freed them from the hands of the devil.
But the holy apostle wished to go on again to other cities and villages as well, to preach the Gospel of Christ.
But that woman, together with all the people, begged him not to leave them, but to teach them the way of the faith day after day.
And the apostle agreed to their request and stayed with them for some time. He taught them the whole way of the faith and of belief, and he appointed for them a bishop,
priests and deacons, and he got ready again to preach the Gospel.
And once again that widow woman and all the Meskhians begged him not to leave them.
But Saint Andrew answered and said to them, "I must preach the Gospel of the Lord in other cities and villages as well." And they said to him:
"If you are leaving, leave that icon of the All-Holy One here with us, as our hope and our protector." The apostle answered and said to them:
"This icon was imprinted by being laid upon the face of the all-holy Mother of God herself
[and so] is [her image]." And he told them everything in order: how, after the Ascension of the Lord, the holy apostles cast lots for the whole earth, to convert it,
and how this land of Samtskhe fell by lot to the all-holy Mother of God,
and that she had sent this icon here as hope and protection for those who had fallen to her lot, and that it was still her will that it remain here permanently, for all ages to come.
When the widow and the Meskhians heard this from the apostle, they were filled with great joy, having learned that they had fallen to the lot of the all-holy Mother of God.
They gave thanks to Christ and to his immaculate Mother, their love and longing for this holy icon grew greater and greater, and they glorified it with tears of joy.
And they placed the all-glorious icon of the all-holy Mother of God of Atskuri in that small [?] church, which is now called the Old Church.
Then the holy apostle Andrew greeted them all with humility and love, gave them his peace, and set out for other places as well to preach the Gospel.
But when King Aderki heard that the Megrelians had abandoned their religion, he was angered and sent his eristavis (governors), and they forced the Megrelians to turn back again.
They hid the icons and crosses. And King Aderki was angry with the eristavi of Klarjeti because he had let the apostle Andrew go in peace.
When the festival of Martvili [?] was over, the glorious Andrew set out from there with the other apostles.
They went from city to city and from village to village, teaching the peoples and working miracles, and in this way they reached the land of Kartli.
Then they crossed the region of Tao, as far as the river Chorokhi, went around all the villages of that region, and preached the name of God without ceasing.
And so, preaching, they reached the land of Svaneti.
In those days a woman ruled that land as its prince, and she believed the apostles' preaching.
Matthias [?] remained in those parts with the other disciples. But the great Andrew, together with Simon, went into the land of Ossetia,
and reached a city called Phokhtapori, where they worked a great miracle and converted and enlightened many people.
From there they went on into the land of Abkhazia and came to the city of Sebastopolis, which is now called Tskhumi.
They preached the word of God to them, and many accepted it.
There the blessed Andrew left Simon the Canaanite with the other disciples, and he himself went up into the land of Jiketi.
The people of that land, the Jiks, were harsh-hearted men, raised in evil deeds, unbelieving and unreceptive [?].
They did not accept the apostle's preaching, but wanted to kill him.
But the grace of God protected him; and when he saw their [?] obstinacy and brutish mind
left them and departed. For this reason they remain in unbelief to this day.
The tomb of Simon the Canaanite is in the city of Nicopsis, between Abkhazia and Jiketi, for Saint Simon the Canaanite died there.
Saint Andrew again strengthened the Megrelians and the Abkhazians in the faith, and he went on to Scythia.
In the reign of this same Aderki, the kingdom of Persia appeared again.
Ever since Alexander had invaded and laid Persia waste, no king had sat on the throne of Persia until this time. Instead, there were Persian eristavis (governors) in one place and another.
Then the eristavis of Persia gathered and set up Azhghalan the Wise as king.

At that time the Armenians and the Georgians were subject to Azhghalan, king of the Persians. Until the reign of Aderki, only one king at a time would sit as king of the Georgians, however many sons the kings had.
This Aderki had two sons: one was named Bartom and the other Kartam.
He divided all his land between them. He gave the city of Mtskheta and the land within the Mtkvari, that is, Inner Kartli: the city on the Mukhnari side and all of Kartli north of the Mtkvari,
from Hereti up to the head of Kartli and Egrisi. All this he gave to his son Bartom. And the city on the Armazi side,
Kartli south of the Mtkvari from Khunani up to the head of the Mtkvari, and all of Klarjeti, he gave to his son Kartam. Then Aderki died.
The eleventh kings: Bartam and Kartam, sons of Aderki, king of the Armenians, Arsacids. His sons reigned after him.
In their reign Vespasian, Caesar of the Romans, captured and plundered Jerusalem. Jews who fled from there came to Mtskheta and settled among the Jews who had been there of old.
Among them were the sons of Barabbas, whom the Jews had released in place of our Lord Jesus at the crucifixion of the Lord.
Bartom and Kartam reigned in peace and in love for one another.
Bartom had a son named Kaos, and Kartam had a son named Parsman. Then Bartom and Kartam, the sons of Aderki, died.
After them their sons became kings: Parsman in Armazi and Kaos in the inner city.
The twelfth kings: Parsman and Kaos, sons of Bartom and Kartam, Arsacids. From Aderki up to their reign, the kings were subject to the king of the Armenians.
The kings of Armazi above all used to help the Armenians against all their enemies. Then the great king Yervand became king in Armenia.

He forgot the good the Georgians had done him. He overpowered Parsman of Armazi and took from the territory of Kartli the city of Tsunda and Artaani as far as the Mtkvari. In Tsunda he settled beast-like men,
of the race of devs (demons), and he named Tsunda Kajatuni, which is translated "house of devs."
The kings of Kartli could not recover the territory, and Parsman and Kaos died in great grief.
After them their sons sat as kings: Azork in Armazi and Armazel in Inner Kartli.
The thirteenth kings: Azork and Armazel, sons of Parsman and Kaos, Arsacids. These kings, Armazel and Azork, were brave and daring men.
They made a pact with each other and resolved to win back the territory of Kartli.
Then Smbat Bivritiani killed Eruand, king of the Armenians, and made Eruand's brother, who was called Artashan, king.

Then these kings of Kartli, Azork and Armazel, called on the Ossetians and the Lekians, and they brought down the kings of the Ossetians, two brothers who were giants, named Bazuk and Abazuk, with the army of Ossetia.
They brought the Pechenegs and the Jiks down with them. The king of the Lekians also came down and brought the Durdzuks and the Didos.
These kings of Kartli gathered their own armies, and this whole countless multitude assembled.
They assembled quickly and in secret, before the armies of the Armenians could gather.
They entered Armenia and, without warning, plundered Shirak and Vanand as far as Bagrevand and Basiani.
Then they turned and plundered the plain as far as Nakhchivan. They took countless captives and spoil, loaded themselves with every kind of goods, and went out by the road of Parisos.
Then Smbat Bivritiani called up the armies of Armenia. The Armenians gathered swiftly and pursued them.
But all these northerners had already crossed the Mtkvari and reached Kambechovani. They had camped on the Iori and were dividing the captives
and the spoil. Then Smbat sent a messenger and said: "The spoil you have taken from Armenia, the livestock, gold, silver and woven goods, I have given all of it to you.
And the blood of the Armenians that you have shed, let that too go unavenged against you.
But release the people you now hold captive, and go in peace, enriched and loaded with every good thing."
But they gave this answer: "We did not enter Armenia for any other purpose than to look for you, and we did not find you.
So now come to us and receive your share. If not, we will come to you wherever you are, and you will not escape from our hands alive."
Then Smbat Bivritiani crossed the Mtkvari. Bazuk, king of the Ossetians, made threats. He sent him a messenger and demanded single combat.
Then Smbat armed himself, mounted his [?] (varsamat), and rode out between the battle lines. Bazuk came out from the other side. Both gave a war cry and charged at each other.
Smbat struck him with his lance at the belt and drove it a cubit out through his back. He lifted him from his horse and threw him to the ground.
Then Ambazuk charged to help his brother. But Smbat pulled the lance out, met him, and struck him the same way and drove it through him. He lifted him and threw him to the ground.
Then he said: "This is for the Armenian mothers and fathers and infant children whom you slaughtered."
Then all those armies of Ossetians, Lekians and Georgians, and all those northern peoples, cried out with one voice and said:
"Since these two brothers, the chief of all the giants, have been killed, our own death counts for nothing."
They became even more savage. They all gathered under the command of Azork and Armazel, the kings of the Georgians, and all of them charged at Smbat and the armies of Armenia.
Then a very great battle took place between them, and the
