battle between them lasted from the third hour until the ninth hour. Countless men fell on both sides. Dust rose up, and the day became as dark as night.
They were mixed together and could no longer recognize one another because of the dust.
Then the army of the North was defeated by the Armenians. They were put to flight and all of them scattered. Smbat went after them,
with many of their many wounded, and he pursued them until nightfall and slaughtered all the Ossetians and the Leks, of whom only a few were left;
but more of the Georgians survived, because they knew the escape routes, and both kings of Kartli fled back to Mtskheta, wounded.
Then Smbat came into Kartli victorious and laid waste to whatever of Kartli he found outside the fortresses and cities;
but he did not attack the fortified cities, because he had set out in haste and was not prepared.
Instead he built a fortress in the land of Odzrkhe, which is called Samtskhe, at a place called Demoti, against the side of Mount Ghado.
He left troops in it to help the people of Tsunda and to fight the people of Odzrkhe, and he departed.
But these kings of Kartli, Arzok and Armazel, were fierce of heart and were not afraid.
Instead they strengthened their fortresses and cities, gave up all the plains of Kartli, and did not stop harassing the Armenians.

The Ossetians began to seek revenge on the Armenians for their blood. They came down into Kartli, made friends with the Georgians, and the Ossetians and Georgians mixed together. And they fought the Armenians constantly.
In the city of Odzrkhe there was an eristavi of King Armazel, one of the nobles, and he stood firm and faithful in his loyalty to Armazel, and
the Mingrelians helped him. The people of Tsunda and of Demoti helped each other. They fought without stopping, and their main fighting usually took place at the river called Noste.
In Klarjeti there was an eristavi of King Arzok, also one of the nobles.
He kept attacking the borders of Armenia, in the land of Parkhali, which is Tao, and no one was able to get into Klarjeti to do it harm.
For it could not be entered and was strong because of its forests and rocks, and the inhabitants of Klarjeti were quick, agile men and horsemen as well.
The kings of Kartli themselves would set out from Mtskheta into Armenia by the road of Abotsi, and so the Georgians kept taking plunder all the time.
Then Artashan, king of the Armenians, marched out with all his forces, together with his commander-in-chief, Smbat Bivritiani.

The Georgians strengthened their fortresses and cities, brought in forces from Ossetia, and filled the fortresses and cities with them. The Armenians came and camped at Mtskheta, and they fought for five months.

Every day there were single combats between champions. Then the Georgians and Ossetians were hard pressed. They asked for peace, and promised to submit and no longer to seek revenge for blood or to dispute the border.
Then the king of the Armenians listened to their plea. They swore oaths and made promises, and the king of the Armenians made the Georgians and Ossetians his subjects, and he departed.
Some number of years passed in this way, and Kartli, which the Armenians had laid waste, was rebuilt.
Then the Armenians were kept busy, because they began a war with the Persians and the Greeks. The Georgians and Ossetians saw this as a good opportunity and began to harass the Armenians.
For all the Armenian troops, the king's two sons and Smbat were away fighting the Persians.
As the Georgians and Ossetians did more and more harm to the Armenians, King Artashan gathered the troops that had stayed at home, gave them to his son Zaren, and sent him against the Georgians.
The Georgians and Ossetians gathered together and went out to meet him in the land of Javakheti.

They joined battle, and the Georgians and Ossetians defeated them. They put to flight Zaren, the son of the king of the Armenians, slaughtered his whole army, and pursued them as far as the border of Armenia.
They overtook Zaren, the king's son, seized him on the shore of the lake called Tseli, and brought him back.
The Ossetians wanted to kill Zaren in revenge for the blood of their kings, but the Georgians kept him alive so that they could use him to demand back their borderlands.
They held him prisoner in the fortress of Darialan. The Armenians could not come after him, because they had no respite from the Persians.
Then, in the third year, Smbat Bivritiani and the king's two sons, Artavazd and Tigran, came with the whole army of Armenia.
Then the kings of Kartli ordered their land to take refuge in the fortresses and cities, and the highlanders fortified the fortresses and cities.

The Armenians came and encamped at Trialeti. Envoys went back and forth between them, and they made peace. The Georgians handed over the captive king's son, and the Armenians promised them help as follows:
"If any enemy rises against you and attacks you from this side, we will both stand with you in person, we two kings, with our army, and help you;
and if, again, you fight against anyone on the other side, we will help you with a thousand armed horsemen at a time."
And the Georgians made this promise in return: "We will strike the drachma in this city of ours with the image of King Artashan."
In return for this the Armenians gave back the borderlands of Kartli: the city of Tsunda and the fortress of Demoti, Javakheti and Artaani.
From then on the Armenians, Georgians and Ossetians became friends, and all three fought their enemies together.
Then Arzok and Armazael died, greatly comforted, because through their valour they had won back the borderlands of Kartli.
After them their sons reigned: Amazasp in Armazi, and Derok in Inner Kartli.
The fourteenth kings: Amazasp and Derok, sons of Azork and Armazael, Arsacids. After them their sons reigned: Pharasmanes Kveli in Armazi, and Mirdat in Inner Kartli.
The fifteenth kings: Pharasmanes Kveli and Mirdat, sons of Amazasp and Derok, Arsacids. Up to this time all these kings, two at a time, had stood in friendship,
at times friends of some and at times enemies of others. Then this Mirdat the Georgian took a Persian wife, a kinswoman of the kings,
and at the instigation of the Persians he became the enemy of Pharasmanes Kveli of Armazi and plotted to kill Pharasmanes Kveli treacherously.
Mirdat invited Pharasmanes Kveli to his house, as if to a banquet and festivity.
But someone told Pharasmanes of this and warned him, and so he did not go.
From then on they became enemies of each other. The Persians helped Mirdat, and the Armenians helped Pharasmanes.
This Mirdat was a cruel and bloodthirsty man. Pharasmanes Kveli, however, was a good man, a generous giver and forgiving, handsome in appearance, tall of stature and strong,
a brave horseman, bold in battle, as fearless as one without a body, and better in every way than all the kings of Kartli who had died before him.

Even the Georgians on Mirdat's side loved him, and they hated Mirdat for his bloodthirstiness and harshness. Most of Mirdat's own followers went over to him; Pharasmanes Kveli grew powerful and drove out King Mirdat.
Mirdat went to Persia. At that time Pharasmanes Kveli's commander-in-chief was a man named Pharnavaz, likewise valiant and a giant,
This Parnavaz was the milk-brother of Parsman: trustworthy, loyal and reliable. And he appointed him over Inner Kartli, in Mirdat's place.
And Parnavaz was always the commander-in-chief within Kartli, while King Parsman the Good travelled about and governed his kingdom.

Then Mirdat brought out the Persians, mighty armies, and marched against Parsman. Parsman gathered the armies of Kartli, brought in forces from Armenia, and went to meet him at the narrows of Rkinis-Khevi (the Iron Gorge).
And the champions began to fight for many days. And if a champion appeared among the Persians whom the champions of Kartli and Armenia could not fight,
King Parsman himself, or his commander-in-chief Parnavaz, would go out against him, and so they would prevail and overcome him.
And in that fighting King Parsman killed seventeen Persian champions, and his commander-in-chief Parnavaz killed twenty-three.
At that time there was a giant among the Persians, named Jumber, who could seize a lion with his hands.
And he challenged King Parsman to single combat. Parsman the Good armed himself joyfully and went out.
And both of them shouted with fierce voices, rushed at each other, and began to fight with swords.
And the noise of their fighting was like the sound of thunder and crashing.
Parsman prevailed: he threw him down and killed him. Then he turned toward his own army, cried out in a loud voice and said to them: "Behold, ravening lions, hail-stricken sheep!"
Then the Georgians and Armenians fell upon the Persians. They put them to flight, slaughtered them, and took countless captives. And Mirdat fled back to Persia.
And in the second year Mirdat came again with a stronger army.
Parsman the Good gathered his armies, horsemen and foot soldiers, and stationed himself inside the city of Mtskheta, because his troops were not as many as Mirdat's troops.
Mirdat came and encamped at Jachvi, and in the same way the champions fought every day.
And in that fighting King Parsman killed twelve champions in single combat, and the commander-in-chief Parnavaz killed sixteen champions.
Then King Parsman, in the ardour of his heart, paid no more heed to the great numbers of the Persians. Instead he went out at dawn with his army and attacked.
And his fortune gave him victory: he routed their camp and slaughtered countless men. And Mirdat fled back to Persia.
And from then on the name of Parsman the Good and of his commander-in-chief Parnavaz became famous. And he became leader of the armies of Kartli and
Armenia. And he began to make war on the Persians and to invade Persia. And no one could ever again stand against Parsman the Good.
Then the Persians devised this trick: they brought a cook, promised him a great reward, and said to him:
"Go and get yourself taken into the service of Parsman the Good. Take deadly poison with you, mix it into his food, and make him eat it."
So that cook went and did as the Persians had told him. And in this way he killed Parsman the Good, the king.
Then there was mourning and weeping, and lamentation with beating of breasts among all the Georgians, from the nobles down to the poor.
And everyone beat themselves in mourning in all the cities and villages, for singers of lament would sit
And they would all gather and recall the courage and valor, the handsomeness and goodness of Pharsman the Brave, and they would speak thus:
"Woe to us, for an evil fate has befallen us, and our king, by whom we had been delivered from slavery to our enemies,
has been killed by [?] sorcerers, and now we have been given over to be plundered by foreign peoples."
Then the Persians came out and brought Mirdat with them, and they seized Kartli and gave Mirdat his share.
But Pharsman's share they took for themselves, and they left an eristavi (governor) at Armazi.
But Pharnavaz the spaspet (commander of the army) took away the wife and son of Pharsman the Brave, and fled, and went to Armenia.
For Pharsman's wife was the daughter of the king of the Armenians. And Mirdat and the Persian eristavi held Kartli.
But the Megrelians remained loyal to Pharsman's son. And at that time the Armenians and the Greeks were friends.
Then the king of the Armenians obtained forces from the Greeks and set out to make war on the Persians and the Georgians.
The Megrelians joined them, and a countless multitude gathered. Then Mirdat and the Persian eristavi obtained forces from Persia.
And the Armenians, the Greeks, and the Megrelians went down into the heart of Kartli, and there the Persians and the Georgians met them at the river called the Liakhvi.
And there a battle took place between them at the place called Rekha.
And countless numbers fell on both sides; the Persians and the Georgians were defeated, and they killed Mirdat and the eristavi of Persia, and slaughtered their troops.
The sixteenth king, Adam, son of Pharsman the Brave, an Arsacid. And they set up as king the son of Pharsman the Brave, whose name was Adam.
And he reigned only three years and died. And his son was left behind, a child one year old;
and while that child was growing up, Adam's mother, the wife of Pharsman the Brave, whose name was Ghadana, reigned.
And when the grandson of Pharsman the Brave, also named Pharsman, had grown up, he reigned.
The seventeenth king, Pharsman, son of Adam, an Arsacid. This Pharsman reigned over all Kartli, and he had a son, and he gave him the name Amazasp.
And after this Pharsman died, and after him his son Amazasp reigned.
The eighteenth king, Amazasp, son of Pharsman, an Arsacid. This Amazasp was a strong man and a great giant, like Pharsman the Brave.
And in his reign the Ossetes came down, great armies, by the road of Dvaleti.
But King Amazasp did not learn of the Ossetes' descent until they had come down over the mountains.
The Ossetes came and camped on the Liakhvi for eight days to rest, and no raiding party went out anywhere, for they had come to destroy the city of Mtskheta.
Then Amazasp summoned all the eristavis of Kartli.
And the eristavis of the east came: the eristavi of Kakheti, the eristavi of Khunani, and the eristavi of Samshvilde.
The spaspet's horsemen gathered. Before the eristavi of the west arrived, the Ossetians came to the northern side of the city, which is Mukhnari.
Then King Amazasp filled the fortresses and gates of Mtskheta with troops.
There was a great number of Mtskheta foot soldiers who guarded the gates and walls. Apart from them, those who went out to fight in the field came to thirty thousand foot soldiers in all.
He also had another ten thousand horsemen. Amazasp went out and stationed the foot soldiers on both sides of the Aragvi, inside the fortifications of the gates.
With the cavalry he went out to the place called Sapurtsle.
He kept the city and the foot soldiers posted inside the gates at his back. And the champions began to fight.
Amazasp went out with a bow and began to shoot with a fierce heart and a strong arm. He shot from so far away that
the Ossetians standing directly opposite did not notice it, and because of the distance they could not even see whether he had a bow at all.
He would shoot arrows that even the strongest armour could not withstand.
On that day Amazasp killed with his own hand fifteen chosen champions and many horses.
Amazasp's other champions also killed many of the Ossetian champions, and they inflicted great harm on the Ossetians.
That day Amazasp came back into the city with the cavalry, but the foot soldiers stayed where they were, inside the gates.
That night more horsemen joined them, ones who had not been able to come with the eristavis because of the haste.
When day broke, Amazasp went out to the same place again and took up a spear.
A man came out from the Ossetians whose name was Khuansua. He was outstanding among the Ossetian troops.
Both of them gave a war cry and charged at each other. At the very first charge Amazasp struck him with the spear, drove it through to his back, and killed him.
He drew his sword and charged at the other champions too, and killed two more. Then he turned back and came into the city together with the horsemen.
The foot soldiers stayed where they were, inside the gates, and that night more horsemen joined them again. Then they decided to attack the Ossetians.

He went out and attacked the Ossetians at dawn with all his cavalry and infantry. He defeated them and put their camp to flight. He killed the king of the Ossetians and slaughtered their whole multitude.
In the second year he took forces from Armenia, gathered all his own troops, and crossed over into Ossetia.
No one could stand against him. He plundered Ossetia and came home victorious.
After this he grew arrogant and began to shed blood, and he killed many nobles.
Because of this the people of Kartli came to hate him. He became an enemy of the Armenians and came to love the Persians.
Then five eristavis of the west rebelled: two eristavis of Egrisi, one of Odzrkhe, one of Klarjeti and one of Tsunda.
They negotiated with the king of the Armenians and asked for his son as their king, for he was Amazasp's sister's son.
Then the king of the Armenians set out for Kartli with a large force, and he also brought in forces from Greece.
They also sent word to the Ossetians, and the Ossetians came gladly, because Amazasp was their blood-enemy.
They crossed over by the road of Takveri and came to the eristavis of Egrisi.
Then Amazasp called on the Persians, and powerful Persians came. He also gathered the Georgians who had remained loyal to him.
Then the Ossetians and the Megrelians crossed over the Lesser Mountains, and they joined the rebel eristavis of Kartli, and all of these came before the king of the Armenians.
Amazasp set out and met them at Gutis-Khevi. Among all those armies of the Greeks
Armenians, Ossetians, Megrelians and Georgians, no one was found to fight Amazasp in single combat. Instead the armies clashed with one another.
A battle took place between them. Amazasp was defeated and his army fled. They killed Amazasp, slaughtered his army and took possession of Kartli.
The king of the Armenians left his own son as king of Kartli. His name was Rev, and he was the son of Amazasp's sister.
The nineteenth king, Rev, an Arsacid. This Rev brought a wife from Greece, the daughter of the logothete, named Sepelia.
This Sepelia brought with her an idol named Aphrodite, and she set it up above Mtskheta.
Although this King Rev was a pagan, he was merciful and a helper to all who were in distress,
because he had heard a little of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ and had some love for Christ.
During his reign he no longer allowed anyone in Kartli to kill children, whom before this time they used to offer as sacrifices to the idols.
As long as he was king, no one killed children for the idols any more. Instead he decreed that sheep and cattle be offered.
For this reason he was called Rev the Just. This Rev reigned well, and then Rev died.
The twentieth king, Vache, son of Rev, an Arsacid. After him his son Vache reigned.
The twenty-first king, Bakur, son of Vache, an Arsacid. After Vache, Vache's son Bakur reigned.
The twenty-second king, Mirdat, son of Bakur, an Arsacid. After Bakur, Bakur's son Mirdat reigned.
The twenty-third king, Aspagur, son of King Mirdat, an Arsacid. After Mirdat his son Aspagur reigned.
This Aspagur built the fortress-city of Ujarma. From the reign of Alexander onward, all these kings reigned in Kartli and were idol-worshippers.
This Aspagur was the last king of the line of the Parnavazids.
At this time Khosrow Anushirvan the Sasanian became king in Persia. He slaughtered the Azhghalanian kings. He is known as Ardabir, as is written in the history of the Persians.
In Armenia Kosaro became king. This Kosaro, king of the Armenians, began to make war on Khosrow, king of the Persians, and Aspagur, king of the Georgians, helped him.
This Aspagur would open the Gates of the Caucasus for him and bring out the Ossetians, the Lekians and the Khazars, and he would go to Kosaro, king of the Armenians, to fight the Persians.
And at their very first entry into Persia, Kasre, the king of the Persians, gave battle, and they put him to flight and slaughtered his army.
And from then on the king of the Persians was no longer able to stand against them, and they made frequent incursions into Persia and plundered Persia.
Now the kings of Kartli of the line of Parnavaz had come to an end,
Chapter Four. The invasion of Kartli by the Persians, and the reign of Mirian son of Kasre. How the Armenians, the Georgians and the northern peoples put the king of the Persians to flight,
and they made frequent incursions into Persia and laid Persia waste; and the king of the Persians was never again able to stand against them.
Then the king of the Persians, full of grief, summoned the rulers of the lands, the pitiakhshes (viceroys) and the eristavis (dukes) of the lands, and held a council.
And he sought a remedy for the evil that had come upon them, and he promised great gifts and honour to whoever could find and devise a means of vengeance.
Now in that assembly there was a certain distinguished prince named Anak, of the kin of Khosrov, the king of the Armenians.
He rose, came forward and said: "Our army has been put to flight by Khosrov, the king of the Armenians, and our horsemen have been destroyed,
and fear and dread of them has fallen upon the Persians, and they have grown strong, and we have no power to stand against them.
Now this is my counsel: that we pacify King Khosrov with peace and entreaty and by paying tribute."
What Anak said he did not say from his heart; rather, he was hiding the plan of his heart from the multitude. He approached the king and said to him privately:
"Listen to me, for what I said is not my counsel; but deem me worthy to speak alone before you, and I will make known to your majesty the plan of my heart."
Then those nobles gave their counsel each in turn before the king and departed. Then the king secretly summoned Anak,
and Anak said to the king: "O king, live forever! I will find for you a means of vengeance upon Khosrov.

I will go to him together with my wife and children; he will trust me because of our kinship, and may your good fortune send me forth well, and I will kill that king, and I will lay down my life for you."
This plan pleased the king. And within a few days Anak and his brother set out with their wives and children, as though defecting from the king of the Persians.
And he came to the borders of Armenia, to the city called Khilakhila, the winter quarters of the kings of the Armenians.
When King Khosrov saw him, he received him with great honour, for Anak made his coming appear trustworthy with every kind of readiness;
and the king saw that he had come to him with his entire household; then the king bestowed honour upon him,
and with joy raised him to the second place beside his own throne. And when they had spent the days of winter in rest, and the days of summer [?] had come,
and the rivers had swollen, the king set out from there and came to the city of Arat; and King Khosrov was preparing to invade Persia again.

Then one day the king went out hunting, and Anak and his brother went along with him, and they carried sharpened swords hidden under their rain-cloaks [?]; and they found their moment, killed the king, and fled.
But the princes of Armenia pursued them, and overtook some at a bridge and others at a ford, and they hemmed them in a narrow place;
and none of them escaped, and they were killed as well. And they slaughtered all their kin, except that two children remained [text breaks off]
…of them, whom their foster-fathers took away: one fled to the borders of Greece and the other to the borders of Persia.
When Kasre (Khosrow) the Sasanian, king of the Persians, heard this news, he was filled with joy and set out with all his forces.
He came first to Armenia and conquered Armenia, and he slaughtered and took captive all the kin of the king of the Armenians.
But one son of King Khosrov, a small boy named Trdat, fled to the borders of Greece and was brought up there.
Then, when the king of the Persians had conquered Armenia and came into Kartli, Aspagur, king of the Georgians, went to Ossetia to gather more troops from Ossetia and to fortify the fortified cities.
But when Aspagur entered Ossetia, death overtook him and he died there.
This Aspagur had no son, only one daughter. Then all the eristavis (dukes) of Kartli gathered in the city of Mtskheta with the spaspet (commander-in-chief), whose name was Maezhan.
Full of grief, they took counsel together and said: "Let us not let grief master our hearts, or our understanding will be taken from us. Instead, let us seek a remedy for our troubles and trials."
Then Maezhan the spaspet said: "If we had enough strength to match even a third of the Persians,
we would give ourselves up to death and resist them. And if an heir of our king, or a kinsman of our kings, had survived
who was worthy of the kingship, we would stand firm inside the fortified cities, give ourselves up to death and eat human flesh, as our fathers did before us.
But the time that has come upon us has brought things to this: the great king of Armenia has been killed by the Persians, and Armenia, on which
our kingdom depended, has been taken, and the king of the Persians has opened his mouth to swallow the whole land.
There is no one among us to stand against him, and we are left orphans, like sheep without a shepherd.
Now this is my counsel: let us offer our submission to the king of the Persians, ask him for mercy, and ask him for his son to be our king,
and let us beg him to marry his son to the daughter of our king Aspagur.
Let us tell him of the girl's descent from the Kartlosids, the Nebrotids, the glorious Arsacids and our kings the Parnavazids,
and let us ask him to keep us in the faith of our fathers, not to mix Persians among us, and to hold us in honour.
Perhaps he will accept this petition of ours and do all this for us. But if he takes the faith of our fathers from us and sets Persians above us,
and destroys the line of our kings, then death is better for us than to see such a thing.
Then let us give ourselves up to death inside the fortresses and cities and all perish."
Then all the eristavis agreed with the counsel of Maezhan the spaspet. They sent an envoy to the king of the Persians and told him everything they had decided.
The king of the Persians first asked about the city of Mtskheta, and they told him how large and strong it was and how near it lay to the Khazars and the Ossetians.
Then he asked about the ancestry of Aspagur's daughter, and they told him of her descent from the Nebrotids, the Arsacids and the Parnavazids.
This pleased the king of the Persians, and he accepted the Georgians' petition, for he himself had already judged it better to set his son in Mtskheta
as king. For of all the cities of Armenia and Kartli, of Ran and its regions,
he chose it above all as the greatest and strongest, and as close to the northern enemies, so that he might fight them from there and hold all the Caucasians in subjection.
He granted everything the Georgians asked for, and gave them an oath and a promise concerning all of it.
And he came to Mtskheta, and Maezhan the spaspet (commander-in-chief) and all the eristavis (dukes) of Kartli came out to meet him.
Then they brought from Samshvilde the daughter of King Aspagur, whose name was Abeshura, and the king of the Persians married her to his son,
who was there with him, seven years old, born of a handmaid; he was called Mihran in Persian and Mirian in Georgian.
This is that Mirian who in the time of his old age came to know God the Creator,
and accepted the Gospel of the apostles through Saint Nino, and became a confessor of the Holy Trinity and a worshipper of the precious Cross.
Chapter Five. The twenty-fourth king, Mirian, son of the king of the Persians.
The Khosroid. Now let us recount the life of Mirian, son of Kasre Ardashir the Sasanian: how King Kasre accepted the petition of the Georgians,
and married his son Mirian to the daughter of the king of the Georgians, and gave his son to the Georgians as king and set him on the throne at Mtskheta.
And he gave him Kartli, Armenia, Ran, Movakan and Hereti. And Mirian was then seven years old.
Mirian's mother was with King Kasre, and he did not leave her with Mirian, for he loved Mirian's mother as his own self;
but he left as foster-father and governor a certain nobleman whose name was
Mirvanoz. And he left forty thousand chosen Persian horsemen, but he did not station those Persians within the borders of Kartli, because of the oath
that he had sworn to the Georgians; instead he stationed them in Hereti, Movakan and Armenia.
But he commanded Mirvanoz to keep seven thousand chosen horsemen from among those Persians in the city at all times as a guard for his son.
And he made this agreement with the Georgians: that the gates, the fortresses and all the cities should be held by Persian troops,
and that no other body of Persians should be in the land of Kartli mingled among the people; "and my son shall be of both religions:
the fire-worship of our fathers and the worship of your idols" — for he had already sworn an oath on this beforehand.
And the king went and subdued all the valleys of the Caucasians, and set rulers everywhere, and commanded all of them to be obedient to his son Mirian;
and he commanded his son Mirian and Mirian's foster-father Mirvanoz to make war on the Khazars. And the king departed for Persia.
And this Mirvanoz strengthened all the fortifications of Kartli, and above all he reinforced the walls of the city of Nekresi.
And Mirian was brought up in the service of those seven idols and of fire.
But he came to love the Georgians, and he forgot the Persian language and learned the Georgian language.

He added to the adornment of the idols and the altars, treated the priests of the idols well, and performed the service of the idols more than all the kings of Kartli. He also adorned the tomb of Parnavaz.
He did all this to win the goodwill of the Georgians, and he treated the Georgians well with gifts and every kind of honour.
And all the Georgians loved him more than all the other kings.
So Mirian reigned from Mtskheta over Kartli across the river, Somkhiti, Ran, Hereti, Movakan and Egrisi.
When Mirian was fifteen years old, his wife, the daughter of the king of the Georgians, died. With her the reign of the Parnavazian kings and queens in Kartli came to an end.
Then all the Georgians grieved over the death of their queen, but they remained loyal to Mirian,
for there was no longer anyone at all of the Parnavazian line who was worthy of the kingship of the Georgians.
For this reason they came to accept Mirian's kingship gladly.
King Mirian added further to the welfare of the Georgians. He brought a wife from Greece, from Pontus: a daughter of Oligotos, named Nana.
He began to fight the Khazars, and he fought them constantly:
whenever the Leks rebelled against Mirian and brought in the Khazars to help them, Mirian went out to meet them in Hereti or Movakan and fought them there;
and whenever they won over the Durdzuks and the Didos and brought in the Khazars, he fought them then too. The Khazars never defeated him, and Mirian always won.
Thus he fought the Khazars many times. His greatest campaigns were at Darubandi (Derbent),
for the Khazars would come and besiege Darubandi, so that they might take it and open the wide gate, and from there begin to march out against the Persians.
Whenever the Khazars came to Darubandi, Mirian would go to the aid of Darubandi. Sometimes the Khazars withdrew from Mirian without a battle, and sometimes he put them to flight in battle.
When Mirian was forty years old, his father, the king of the Persians, died, and Mirian's younger brother, whose name was Bartam, sat as king of Persia after him.
When Mirian heard this, he called up all his troops, gathered them, and set out for Baghdad, so that he might sit on his father's throne.
Then his brother gathered countless troops and came out to meet him in battle at the valley of Nasibin (Nisibis).
When the elders and marzpans of Persia saw that the sword was about to fall upon one another, they stood up between them as envoys and judges, and both kings agreed to accept their judgement.
When they sat down to judge, Mirian argued his case: "I am my father's firstborn son, and foreign lands, won by the strength of my arm, were given to me as my princely portion,
and there I have spent all my days fighting the Khazars, and many times I have defended Persia from the Khazars with my own blood.
Therefore my father's throne is mine." But Bartam said in reply:
"Even if Mirian is the firstborn, he is the son of a slave woman, and it is enough of a lot for the son of a slave woman that kingdoms have fallen to him.
I, however, am the son of the daughter of the king of the Indians, the queen of the Persians. You have heard my father's will, and you have seen that he set the crown on my head with his own hand."
They gave their judgement and granted the kingship of Persia to Bartam. To satisfy Mirian, they had Bartam give him Jazireti (Upper Mesopotamia), half of Shami (Syria), and Adarbadagan (Azerbaijan).
And all of these were added to Kartli, Armenia, Ran, Hereti and Movakan. And Mirian came back. But while Mirian was still there, the Ossetians

Perosh and Kavtia came over the mountains and ravaged Kartli. But Mirian crossed into Ossetia by an outer route, plundered Ossetia and reached as far as Khazaria, and came back over the road of Dvaleti and returned home.
And some years after this the Khazars came, as was their custom, to fight for Darubandi (Derbent).
And Mirian went to help Darubandi, and while he was there fighting the Khazars, the king of the Goths invaded Greece with a countless army.
And the king of the Greeks gathered a great army and opposed him.
Then the king of the Goths challenged the emperor to single combat. But the emperor was not able to fight him.

Now there was at that time with the Greek army the son of Kosaros (Khosrov), king of the Armenians, named Trdat (Tiridates), whom we mentioned above. He had been brought up in Greece, and he was a giant.
At that time he was with the Greek army, and they chose him out of the whole Greek army,
and they clothed him in the emperor's clothing and armour, and sent him, in the guise of the emperor, to fight the king of the Goths.
The king of the Goths came out from his side, and they attacked each other in combat. Trdat won and took him captive with his own hands, and they routed the camp of the Goths.
And the emperor gave troops to Trdat and sent him to Armenia, his homeland. They came to Armenia and drove out the troops and the eristavis (governors) of Mirian.
Then Mirian returned from the war with the Khazars, and brought from Persia a kinsman of his, of the royal family, named Peroz; and he brought a great army with him.
And Mirian gave this Peroz his daughter as wife, and gave him the land from Khunani to Bardav,
on both sides of the Mtkvari (Kura), and set him there as eristavi. And he brought other forces too from Persia and began to make war on Trdat.
And whenever Trdat brought forces from Greece and came against Mirian, Mirian could not stand against him, and he would fortify his fortresses and cities, and Trdat would overrun his land.
And whenever Mirian grew strong with help from Persia, then Trdat could not stand against him, and Mirian would overrun Armenia.
And so there was unceasing strife between them for many years, and no one was ever found among the Persians who could match Trdat in single combat.
And he became famous in every land, and he defeated all his opponents, as his story is written in the History of the Armenians.
After this the third brother of Mirian and Bartam became king in Persia. He sent an envoy to Mirian and said:
"Let us join forces, cross through Armenia, and invade Greece."
Then the king of the Persians set out, and Mirian met him, and a countless multitude gathered, like the grass of the fields and the leaves of the trees in number.
And they crossed through Armenia, and Trdat could not stand against them, but fortified his fortresses and cities. And they plundered Armenia and invaded Greece.
And Constantine, king of the Greeks, could not stand against them, and he fell into great distress.
And when they began to plunder Greece, certain God-fearing men persuaded King Constantine, saying:
"We have seen the wonders of Christ and the victory over enemies won by those who trust in him: how all who trust in Christ defeat their enemies when the cross is carried before them."
But King Constantine came to believe as they did [lit. "believed theirs"], as is written plainly in the Conversion of the Greeks.

Constantine was baptized. He carried the sign of the cross before him and, with a small army, joined battle with the countless hosts of his Persian enemies. By the power of Christ he routed their camp and slaughtered their multitude.
Both kings fled with a few horsemen, and Constantine pursued them and entered their territory.
The king of the Persians fled back into Persia, but Mirian stayed in Kartli and fortified his fortress-cities.
Mirian was left without resources and feared that he would be driven out of Kartli entirely, for all his nobles, both Persians and Georgians, had been destroyed in that battle.
Therefore he sent an envoy to King Constantine and asked him for peace. He promised to serve him, to break away from the Persians and to side with him.
This pleased Constantine, for he still feared the king of the Persians, and he made peace with Mirian in order to have his help.
He took Mirian's son, whose name was Bakar, as a hostage. He reconciled Trdat and Mirian and made them related to each other by marriage.
For Trdat gave his daughter, whose name was Salome, as a wife to Mirian's son, whose name was Rev.
He set the border between Mirian and Trdat as follows: the lands whose rivers flow southward and join the Araxes he assigned to Trdat's share;
and the lands whose rivers flow northward and join the Mtkvari (Kura) he assigned to Mirian's share.
When King Constantine had settled this and acted as mediator between them, he went back to his own kingdom. Mirian reigned there over Kartli, Ran, Hereti and Movakan.
He also held Egrisi as far as the Egris River. He gave his son Rev Kakheti as his princely appanage, and
Kukheti, and he settled him at Ujarma: Rev and his wife Salome, the daughter of Trdat. They lived at Ujarma.
Peroz, Mirian's son-in-law, held the land that we mentioned above as given to him by Mirian, and he was eristavi there.
At that time our holy and blessed mother and baptizer Nino had come, and she had stayed in Mtskheta for three years and made known the praise of the faith of Christ.
She performed healings without medicine, and in a loud voice she began to praise the true faith of Christ our God.
